newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-RANGERS AIM TO BREAK HEARTS ONCE AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-RANGERS AIM TO BREAK HEARTS ONCE AGAIN.

text.p: Like the three kings of the Scriptures, Saturday's pre-Christmas Scottish league clash between Heart of Midlothian and Rangers promises to deliver three things -- not gold, frankincense and myrrh, but goals, red cards and broken Hearts.
The last three encounters between these two sides, all in different competitions, have been remarkable for different reasons.
The only constant is that Hearts, so often the nearly-team of Scottish football, have finished as the losing side.

When the two rivals met in the Scottish Cup final in May Rangers were unstoppable, snuffing out Hearts' dreams of their first trophy in 34 years with a crushing 5-1 victory crafted by Dane Brian Laudrup.
He scored twice and set up a Gordon Durie hat-trick as the defending Scottish champions waltzed to their 27th Scottish Cup title.

Hearts' afternoon was summed up by Rangers' second goal when French goalkeeper Gilles Rousset stooped to collect an ineffectual cross from Laudrup and inexplicably let it trickle through his legs into the net. All in all, an afternoon to forget for the Edinburgh side.
The next clash was in the league at Ibrox in September. Rangers established a 1-0 lead in an uneventful first half before Hearts' world collapsed around their heads after the interval.

Their Italian defender Pasquale Bruno was sent off, Paul Gascoigne extended Rangers' lead, and then, in an insane seven minutes, Hearts' David Weir, Neil Pointon and Paul Ritchie were all dismissed for crimes ranging from late tackles to "violent conduct" to "use of foul and abusive language".
Rangers looked almost embarrassed as they played out the remaining 20 minutes against the seven of Hearts, adding just one more goal for a 3-0 victory.
When the sides met again in this season's League Cup final Hearts fought back from 2-0 down to 2-2 and threatened to over-run Rangers.

Enter Paul Gascoigne, Rangers' erratic England midfielder. Two waves of Gazza's magic right boot in the space of three minutes and the Glaswegians were back in control, leading 4-2 with less than half an hour to play.
By the time Weir pulled one back for Hearts in the 90th minute, Rangers fans were already celebrating their 19th League Cup win. Gascoigne had left Hearts broken-hearted again.
Nobody would suggest Hearts against Rangers represents the fiercest rivalry in Scottish football. That award goes to the Old Firm clash between Rangers and Glasgow rivals Celtic.
But any clash between sides from Glasgow and Edinburgh raises passions in the country's two biggest cities, which glare at each other across southern Scotland as if from different worlds.
Glasgow, steeped in working-class tradition and divided on religious lines like no other city on the British mainland, lies at the heart of Scotland's old industrial heartland.
It was out of the city's Protestant community in the late 19th century that Rangers Football Club was born.

Edinburgh, the capital and traditional seat of power, is more elegant and more prosperous than its neighbour. It size, compared to Glasgow, is reflected in its more modest football teams -- Hibernian and Hearts.

Modesty will not prevent Hearts seeking revenge against the defending Scottish champions but, having won only four of the 20 league encounters against Rangers over the past five seasons, Jim Jeffries's side will be well aware history is stacked against them.
And although it is nearly Christmas, Hearts can be sure that when the undisputed kings of Scottish football arrive at Tynecastle Park on Saturday, they will not be bearing seasonal gifts.
